opposingBeliefs: Vegans are always deficient in nutrients
Meat is essential for strength and muscle
mainClaim: Well-planned plant-based diets reduce risk of heart disease, diabetes, and certain cancers more effectively than omnivorous diets
evidence: The Adventist Health Study-2 (Orlich and coauthors, JAMA Internal Medicine, 2013) followed 73,308 participants and found that vegetarian dietary patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality than non-vegetarian patterns (hazard ratio 0.88), with a significant association for cardiovascular mortality. No verified source is cited for the other claims about plant-based diets in this argument.
supportingPoints: Position of Academy of Nutrition: plant-based diets appropriate for all life stages
Lower LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, BMI in vegetarians vs omnivores
Fiber intake 2-3x higher prevents colorectal cancer and improves gut health
No dietary requirement for meat; B12 easily supplemented (even meat-eaters often deficient)
Environmental benefits: 75% less land use, 66% less water, 49% less GHG emissions
Ethical considerations: reduces animal suffering in factory farms
limitations: The earlier Lancet meta-analysis could not be traced to a published source and was removed, as were the 24%, 50% and 3-6 years figures attributed to the Adventist study, which its paper does not report. Other figures in the supporting points have not been checked. Requires careful planning for B12, iron, omega-3s, vitamin D. Some people may have difficulty digesting high-fiber diets initially. Not all plant-based foods are healthy (Oreos are vegan). Individual responses vary. Supplementation may be needed. Social challenges in meat-centric cultures.
counterCounterArguments: Supplements are widely available and inexpensive
Meal planning apps make nutrition tracking easy
Growing availability of fortified plant-based products
